name: Projected value
first: A second value that a property wrapper can give for each property it is used on, read by writing a dollar sign before the property's name.

dependsOn.why: A projected value belongs to a property wrapper, and is read through a property that uses the wrapper.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `game.$score` reads the projected value of `AtMostTen`, the property wrapper that `Game` uses on `score`.

sil.shows: Reading $score reads the projectedValue of the AtMostTen that each Game keeps for score.

what.is: A projected value is a second value that a property wrapper can give for each property it is used on, beside the property's own value. Code reads it by writing a dollar sign before the property's name.
what.afterExample: The property wrapper `AtMostTen` gives `score` a projected value, which is true when the last value written to `score` was more than 10. Line 18 reads it as `game.$score`.
what.problem: A property wrapper sometimes has more to tell about a property than its value, such as whether it changed the value it was given. A property gives only one value, of its own type. A projected value gives a second value, of any type, through the same property's name.
what.how: swiftc gives `Game` a second property, `$score`, beside `score`. Reading `game.$score` reads the `projectedValue` of the instance of `AtMostTen` that `game` keeps for `score`.

when.text: Use one in SwiftUI to give another view a value that a view keeps, so that the other view can change it. The projected value of `@State` is a `Binding`, which reads and writes the state's value:
Use one in your own property wrapper when it has a second value to give, such as `AtMostTen`'s `projectedValue`, which tells whether the last value was more than 10.
Don't add one when the wrapped value says everything. A property wrapper needs only `wrappedValue`. Writing `$` before the name of a property whose wrapper has no projected value does not build.

parts.name: The property `projectedValue`, line 4
parts.text: Line 4 declares `projectedValue`, a property of the property wrapper `AtMostTen`. A property wrapper that has a property with this name has a projected value, of any type. Here it is a Boolean, and it starts as `false`. Line 9, in the setter of `wrappedValue`, sets it to true when `newValue` is more than 10, and to false when it is not.

parts.name: The dollar sign, in `$score`
parts.text: A dollar sign before the name of a wrapped property reads the wrapper's projected value, in place of its wrapped value. So on line 18, `game.$score` reads the `projectedValue` of the instance of `AtMostTen` that keeps `score`. On line 20, `game.score` reads its `wrappedValue`.

steps.text: Line 16 makes a `Game`, and stores it in `game`. Its instance of `AtMostTen` for `score` starts with `number` set to 0 and `projectedValue` set to `false`.
Line 17 writes 4 to `game.score`. That runs the setter of `wrappedValue`, with `newValue` set to 4.
Line 8 stores 4 in `number`. 4 is not more than 10, so line 9 sets `projectedValue` to false.
Line 18 reads `game.$score`, the `projectedValue` of the instance of `AtMostTen` for `score`. Line 18 prints {{false}}.
Line 19 writes 25 to `game.score`, and the setter runs again, with `newValue` set to 25.
Line 8 stores 10 in `number`, because 10 is smaller than 25. 25 is more than 10, so line 9 sets `projectedValue` to true.
Line 20 reads `game.score`, which is 10, and `game.$score`, which is true. Line 20 prints {{10 true}}.

end.text: A projected value is a second value of a property wrapper. `game.score` reads the wrapper's `wrappedValue`, and `game.$score` reads its `projectedValue`.
